analysis.title: What Rate Moves Really Mean for Commercial Real Estate Cap Rates
key_insights: The 10-year Treasury approached its highest level since 2002 after a September 2026 Fed rate hike and renewed energy-driven inflation. Private real estate investors are asking what this means for values they cannot yet observe.

MIM's Public Market Signals framework from May 2025 still applies: Baa corporate yields and the two-year Treasury explain about 80% of the variation in NCREIF transaction cap rates, with public markets leading private pricing by about two quarters.
If rates stay at current levels, the model implies transaction cap rates about 30 bps above Q2 2026 levels (5.9% to 6.2%). That is roughly half the 70-bp rise in the 10-year Treasury.

The 10-year Treasury is the wrong benchmark. Between 2021 and end-2023 it rose 4.5 percentage points while transaction cap rates rose about 2 percentage points. It misses risk spreads and property income growth.
Baa yields push cap rates up almost one-for-one. The two-year Treasury carries a negative coefficient because inflation lifts future rents and property income.

A 30-bp rise in modeled cap rates holding income constant equates to a value decline of about 5%, versus about 10% under a one-for-one 10-year benchmark. MIM treats 5% as an upper bound, since rates would need to hold for at least a quarter and rate pressure is expected to moderate as inflation eases later this year and into 2027.

The REIT market appears to agree, with prices off roughly 2% from their second-quarter average. This is a growth-driven rise in rates with credit spreads still tight, a combination real estate has historically weathered well.

Modeled cap rates are more than halfway to the 50-bp threshold set in the original report for a more risk-off posture on new investments. MIM sees this as a 'yellow' signal and is adjusting underwriting assumptions.

Credit spreads are the variable to watch. A recession that widened Baa spreads would hurt modeled cap rates more than further Fed hikes, because falling Treasury yields offer less protection than tightening credit removes.
The May 2025 signals indicated the tariff shock barely moved real estate pricing. NCREIF transaction cap rates in mid-2026 were essentially the same as mid-2025, which MIM says confirmed its view.

sector_views.rationale: Modeled cap rates up about 30 bps implies a value decline of about 5% at most, less than a 10-year-based heuristic suggests. MIM calls the signal 'yellow' and is adjusting underwriting.

macro_indicators.interpretation: First Fed hike since 2023, following three cuts in late 2025 and a re-acceleration of inflation after a Middle East energy shock.
Near the highest level since 2002, driven by heavy issuance and fiscal deficit concerns raising term premiums.
Proxy for near-term inflation expectations and Fed policy. Carries a negative coefficient in the cap rate model.
Reflects the risk-free rate and credit spreads and is the dominant driver of modeled cap rates.
Model estimate if yields stay at current levels. Actual transaction pricing lags public markets by about two quarters.
Middle East energy shock pushed oil above $100 and re-accelerated inflation, prompting the Fed to reverse course.

risk_factors: A recession that widened Baa credit spreads would damage modeled cap rates more than further Fed hikes.
Rates holding at current levels for more than a quarter would exert their full effect on transaction pricing.
Heavy Treasury issuance and rising U.S. fiscal deficit concerns are pushing term premiums higher.
Renewed energy-driven inflation could keep rates elevated longer than MIM's base case of moderation.

tension_points.bull_case: Modeled cap rates rise only about 30 bps against a 70-bp rise in the 10-year, implying a value decline of about 5% at most. Rate pressure is expected to moderate as inflation eases later this year and into 2027. REITs are off only about 2%, and credit spreads remain tight.
tension_points.bear_case: Modeled cap rates are more than halfway to the 50-bp risk-off threshold. A recession that widened Baa spreads would do far more damage than further Fed hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A widening of Baa credit spreads in a recession, or modeled cap rates reaching the 50-bp rise threshold set in the original report.

theme_stances.key_argument: Cap rates should rise about half as much as the 10-year Treasury, because Baa yields and the two-year Treasury are better benchmarks.
A recession that widened Baa spreads would do far more damage to modeled cap rates than further Fed hikes.
theme_stances.evidence: Credit spreads matter as much as Fed policy does
